subject: Tenant egress mitigation and attack-path walkthrough for Atlas RFP
messages:
From: Lenora Bates <lenora.bates@atlasfin.com>
To: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>
Cc: procurement@atlasfin.com
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 09:17:00 -0700
Subject: RFP: Data-plane egress & east-west isolation questions

Vanessa,

Thanks for the quick intro call last week. Atlas is collecting a short written response for our security review board focused on multi-tenant egress controls and east-west isolation for inference workloads. Could you please provide the following so we can close round 1 of the RFP?

1) A network-level diagram showing tenant isolation boundaries for both hosted and private deployment modes (data plane and control plane).
2) A matrix of egress destinations allowed per-tenant (service accounts, external SaaS, telemetry endpoints) and the enforcement point (egress proxy/bastion/firewall).
3) A brief threat-model summary mapping likely attack paths to mitigations (especially around KV cache leakage and model artifact exfiltration).
4) Any noteworthy deviations for VPC/private deployments (bastion, NAT, customer-managed routing).

If possible, please attach supporting diagrams and a short walkthrough we can present at our next security gate on Wednesday (May 12). We prefer PDFs and spreadsheets for internal consumption.

Thanks,
Lenora Bates
Senior Security Engineer
Atlas Financial
lenora.bates@atlasfin.com
[atlasfin.com]

Subject: Re: RFP: Data-plane egress & east-west isolation questions

Hi Lenora — thanks for the clear list. We're preparing a concise package that addresses each bullet and can present a 30-minute walkthrough on Wed the 12th. Preliminary attachments below; final versions to follow after an internal technical review:

- redwood-data-plane-segmentation-v1.png (high-level diagram, shows control vs data plane, tenant projection, egress proxy)
- egress-policy-matrix_v2.xlsx (per-tenant allowed destinations, enforcement points, justification)
- attack-path-walkthrough-notes.pdf (threat-model summary + mitigations)

High-level notes here:
- Hosting modes: hosted API uses our managed VPCs with tenant-level overlay isolation and an egress proxy cluster. Private (VPC) deployments can either adopt Redwood-managed egress proxies (for siloed tenants) or use customer-managed NAT/gateway; we call that out in the matrix.
- Enforcement: egress is enforced at multiple layers — host firewall (iptables/nft), service mesh policies for intra-cluster east-west, and a centralized egress proxy that performs destination allowlisting and TLS interception for approved telemetry endpoints (mutually-auth TLS for internal endpoints).
- KV/cache risk: KV caches are per-tenant process-scoped; we do not persist caches to shared storage. Access to model artifacts and KV material is mediated by RBAC + short-lived credentials; we include rotation cadence in the notes.

Karthik/Marissa — can you please validate the attached diagram and matrix before close of day so I can send the final set to Atlas? Jonas, if you have any red-team observations from the last tabletop, add them here.

— Vanessa
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Fwd: RFP: Data-plane egress & east-west isolation questions — internal review

Folks — forwarding Lenora's request and the draft attachments. Key asks from SecOps: diagram, per-tenant egress matrix, and a short attack-path mapping. Below are the engineering notes I think we should include verbatim in the final doc — please edit for tone and accuracy.

Karthik's notes (edited):
- Tenant isolation: we run logical tenants as separate runtime sandboxes inside the serving fleet. Each sandbox gets a unique runtime UID + namespace. Network namespaces are leveraged at the host-level to ensure process isolation; we also mount ephemeral filesystem for model artifacts scoped per-runtime.
- Egress enforcement chain: 1) service-level allowlists inside the runtime (application config), 2) host-level firewall (deny by default, allow by explicit rules), 3) egress proxy for outbound HTTP(s) with allowlisting and header stripping, 4) centralized DLP hooks for attachments or blob exits to external storage. This layered approach defends against misconfigurations and compromised workloads.
- East-west: service mesh policies restrict model-serving instances to talk only to data-plane infrastructure (KV, logging, metrics). Cross-tenant traffic is dropped by default. For internal admin channels we use mTLS with client certs rotated daily for ephemeral sessions.
- Attack-path considerations: the most plausible is a compromised tenant process attempting to use the egress proxy to exfiltrate model artifacts. Mitigations: per-tenant destination allowlists, per-tenant mTLS for telemetry, token scoping, and agent-side content scanning. Also we recommend optional customer-managed egress for regulated customers (no shared proxy).

Marissa's notes (edit suggestions):
- Add explicit statement: we don't allow arbitrary outbound S3 endpoints — only pre-approved storage buckets.
- Provide a short table listing fallback behaviors during egress-proxy outage (fail-closed vs fail-open per contract). Our standard is fail-closed for hosted enterprise customers; for private we document the chosen behavior in the deployment runbook.

Jonas — any red-team flags or phrasing you want to add? Please reply in-thread. I’ll fold comments into the final PDF.

— Vanessa

From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa.ortiz@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: RFP: Data-plane egress & east-west isolation questions — package + walkthrough

Hi Lenora — attaching the finalized artifacts for your security gate. Thank you for the checklist; we incorporated Atlas' request for explicit fail-closed behavior and included an optional private-deployment diagram that shows customer-managed NAT/bastion.

What we attached:
- redwood-data-plane-segmentation-v1.png — high-level diagram with separate control and data planes, tenant namespaces, and egress-proxy placement. See legend for colors: orange (tenant runtime), blue (control plane), green (shared infra).
- egress-policy-matrix_v2.xlsx — per-tenant allowed destinations, enforcement layer (runtime/host/proxy), justification, and failover mode. Notable rows:
  * telemetry.redwood.internal (mutual TLS) — allowed for all tenants, enforced at proxy + service mesh
  * s3.redwood-models (internal storage) — read-only for serving runtimes, enforced via signed short-lived URLs and token scoping
  * external-storage (customer-managed) — only allowed if customer opts into managed egress; otherwise blocked
- attack-path-walkthrough-notes.pdf — concise threat model summary and numbered attack-path walkthrough (initial compromise -> attempt to enumerate KV -> attempt to reach external storage via proxy -> exfiltrated content). For each path we list detection signals (anomalous egress rates, missing mTLS certs) and mitigations (token scope, DLP hooks, host firewall).

Key clarifications for Atlas:
- KV/cache: ephemeral, per-runtime, never mounted on shared persistent storage. Access scoped by short-lived credentials with 5 minute TTLs for serving nodes.
- Failover behavior: hosted enterprise customers use fail-closed by default for egress proxy; private deployments document customer choice in runbooks.
- Admin access: all operator/admin paths require customer-initiated approval (RBAC) and are logged to immutable audit streams retained per contract.

Next steps: we can demo the attack-path walkthrough and the diagram on Wed May 12 at 11:00am PT (we're holding a 30-minute slot) — does that work for your team? If you want more technical depth, Karthik can drop into the call and walk the red-team scenarios.

Links: detailed doc set is in the shared drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1bEgressMatrixAtlas

Regards,
Vanessa Ortiz
